newsitem.title: UK: NWE fuel cargoes higher with transatlantic demand.
newsitem.headline: NWE fuel cargoes higher with transatlantic demand.

text.p: High sulphur fuel oil barges ended on Monday a little weaker on low demand after fetching higher numbers earlier in the day, while cargoes were talked higher with Russian material said to be moving transatlantic.

High sulphur fuel barges moved down to trade at $85 fob ARA after earlier trading at $86, or some 50 cents to 75 cents over Friday's close. The weak bunker demand, put by many traders at 10,000 tonnes, was said to have weakened the market and late talk was $84/$85.
Low sulphur barges were very dull, unchanged from last week's $95/$97 a tonne range.

However, high sulphur cargoes were offered higher as the day progressed at the $85 cif region, with swaps up and after barges went up early in the day. Bids came in at $83 but no deals were heard done.
Traders said the market was pushed up by Russian supply continually being absorbed by the market and with an open transatlantic arb.
"They (cargoes) rose due to the Russian stuff which is being absorbed and with the open arb to the States," one seller said, adding that a lot of the fuel oil shipments were going into Mexico.
"Refiners there are in turnaround that's why they've been buying throughout the summer," the seller added.
But one trader said that most of the Mexican demand has been covered, adding he was offered lower quality cracked material at $81 and $79 cif.
One percent was largely steady with a 20,000-tonne cargo traded at $94 fob.
The buyer, a trader, said several cargoes were still available in the North but buying interest was coming in from the Mediterranean.
However, other traders said the price was intentionally kept high to price a cargo to go out of the region.
One seller was heard offering at high fob plus $1.75 for a July 15-20 loader, and a bid came in a few dollars lower.

"I think people are looking whether it works across to the United States on one percent which on paper it appears to. It's going to take a couple of days to know what the direction of the market ought to be," a trader with a major said.
"The states is giving a floor to one percent," he added.
